articles.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.
articles.content:
Carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

The discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

Beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

Scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

Recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

These plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

When that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam says.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature

Hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

The Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," says Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core."

Although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created."

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

"All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets."

Scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The new findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially important contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

According to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth

Despite the intriguing evidence, important questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

"We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

They also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

"It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting."

The study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.

This breakthrough enhances understanding of planetary formation and Earth's deep carbon cycle, with broad implications for science and humanity's knowledge of life’s origins. The story is focused, detailed, and has meaningful real-world impact by advancing knowledge about Earth's environment and life-supporting processes.

Over time, this carbon traveled up through the planet’s layers and came out through volcanoes.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it links carbon essential for life to materials from space and Earth's deep interior. It shows that some carbon may have taken a long journey from meteorites, into the core, and then back to the surface. This helps scientists understand how Earth formed and how life’s building blocks arrived.

articles.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
articles.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.
articles.content:
For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today. A new scientific analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere during three major stages, while the deep oceans took much longer to catch up. In some cases, the delay stretched across hundreds of millions of years, with the final transition involving a gap of roughly 600 million years.

Two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation. Their findings challenge the traditional understanding of Earth's oxygen history by examining chemical evidence that reflects conditions in the ancient atmosphere rather than relying primarily on measurements of ocean chemistry.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Different Oxygen Timeline

Scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments. However, the amount of oxygen in seawater is influenced by many factors besides the atmosphere, including nutrient availability, biological productivity, ocean circulation, and the shapes of ocean basins. This makes ocean chemistry an imperfect guide to conditions in the air.

The researchers instead focused on sulfate, a chemical compound that can preserve a distinctive signal from atmospheric oxygen. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere produce an unusual shortage of the oxygen isotope oxygen-17. When sulfide minerals undergo weathering, this chemical fingerprint is transferred into sulfate, which can eventually become preserved in sedimentary rocks. By examining these signatures, scientists can gain a more direct picture of how atmospheric oxygen changed over time.

According to this evidence, Earth's first major increase in oxygen occurred during the Great Oxidation Event, between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen rose from less than one-millionth of today's concentration to somewhere between 0.1% and 10% of modern levels.

The second major increase took place approximately 1.3 billion to 1.0 billion years ago, followed by a third between 440 million and 410 million years ago. Both occurred earlier than conventional timelines suggest.

Under this interpretation, the well-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, traditionally dated to 800 million to 500 million years ago and 420 million to 360 million years ago, mainly reflect delayed changes in ocean oxygen levels. The oceans responded roughly 200 million and 30 million years after the corresponding atmospheric increases.

Earth's Atmosphere and Oceans Did Not Always Change Together

Despite these major increases, oxygen remained relatively scarce throughout much of Earth's history. Models based on the isotope evidence suggest that atmospheric oxygen during the middle Proterozoic reached only about 0.1% to 1% of present-day levels.

Another clue comes from the fossil record of charcoal. Because charcoal formation requires atmospheric oxygen concentrations of approximately three-quarters of modern levels, its absence from older rocks suggests that oxygen remained too scarce to support widespread burning. Charcoal first appears in the geological record around 420 million years ago.

The researchers also highlight a surprising relationship between oxygen in the atmosphere and oxygen in the oceans. Over extremely long periods, the two generally increased together. However, on timescales of around a million years, they could move in opposite directions.

When additional oxygen entered the oceans, it could react with accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, consuming oxygen in the process. These reactions could reduce the amount of oxygen remaining in the atmosphere.

As a result, some chemical signals previously interpreted as evidence of rising oxygen may actually record periods when atmospheric oxygen was declining. This possibility could change how scientists interpret major fluctuations in Earth's ancient oxygen record.

Oxygen-Rich Oases Existed Billions of Years Ago

The spread of oxygen through Earth's oceans was also far from uniform. The researchers describe two major sources of oxygen in seawater: oxygen produced locally by photosynthetic microorganisms and oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere.

The first process created isolated pockets of oxygen-rich water as early as 3 billion years ago, possibly even earlier. These small oxygenated environments existed during the Archean, when the atmosphere and most of the oceans still contained very little free oxygen.

As atmospheric oxygen levels gradually increased, oxygen entering seawater from the air became more important. Eventually, this atmospheric supply overtook local biological production as the dominant mechanism driving widespread ocean oxygenation.

Even then, the transformation was remarkably slow. According to the proposed timeline, the deep ocean did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago, long after oxygen had begun accumulating in the atmosphere.

How Rising Oxygen Changed the Evolution of Life

These findings also offer a new perspective on the relationship between oxygen and the evolution of complex organisms.

When Earth's atmosphere contained virtually no oxygen, its absence placed a major restriction on oxygen-dependent life. During the Proterozoic, increasing oxygen availability gradually made new environments accessible, although concentrations continued to fluctuate as early animals evolved.

Rather than acting as a single trigger for complex life, oxygen initially provided opportunities for biological innovation. Only after the third major atmospheric increase did higher oxygen levels become a powerful force supporting greater biological complexity.

This later transformation helped create conditions favorable for larger animals, more active predators, and organisms capable of occupying deeper marine environments.

The researchers acknowledge that important uncertainties remain. The available isotope record does not capture every change in detail, and absolute atmospheric oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain difficult to establish. Additional increases or decreases may have occurred without leaving sufficiently clear chemical evidence to identify them.

Nevertheless, the analysis proposes a major revision to the sequence of events that transformed Earth into an oxygen-rich planet. Rather than the oceans becoming oxygenated first and the atmosphere following, the evidence suggests that atmospheric oxygen increased well before the deep oceans responded.

That prolonged delay may have played an important role in shaping the environments where complex life emerged and evolved.
articles.reasoning: The article presents a significant scientific breakthrough revising the timeline of Earth's oxygenation, which has broad implications for understanding the evolution of life and Earth's environmental history. This new understanding of atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels offers meaningful insight into planetary conditions that enabled complex life, impacting multiple scientific fields and public knowledge about Earth's environment.
articles.personality_title: New study reshapes timeline of Earth's oxygen rise and its impact on life
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For billions of years, Earth had almost no oxygen in its atmosphere, making it very different from today. Scientists have long studied when and how oxygen levels increased, helping life become more complex.

**What happened** – Two researchers from Chengdu University of Technology analyzed ancient rocks in a new way. Instead of focusing on ocean chemistry, they studied sulfate chemicals that carry clues about atmospheric oxygen. Their findings show that oxygen in the atmosphere rose in three main stages: about 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago, 1.3 to 1.0 billion years ago, and 440 to 410 million years ago. The oceans, however, took much longer—sometimes hundreds of millions of years—to gain oxygen after the atmosphere did.

**Impact** – This research changes how we understand Earth's oxygen history. It shows that the atmosphere became rich in oxygen well before the deep oceans did. This delay helps explain why complex life took time to develop and why some earlier signs of oxygen were misleading. It also reveals that small oxygen-rich areas existed in the oceans billions of years ago, even when most of the planet was oxygen-poor.

**What's next step** – Scientists will use this new timeline to rethink how oxygen shaped life’s evolution. They will look for more detailed chemical evidence to fill gaps and better understand oxygen’s role in Earth's past. This could lead to new discoveries about how life survived and changed under shifting oxygen levels.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New evidence shows Earth's atmosphere gained oxygen long before the deep oceans did, reshaping our understanding of how oxygen influenced the rise of complex life.

Les océans, cependant, ont mis beaucoup plus de temps – parfois des centaines de millions d'années – à s'oxyder après l'atmosphère.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio cambia la cronología del aumento de oxígeno en la Tierra y su impacto en la vida
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante miles de millones de años, la Tierra tenía casi nada de oxígeno en su atmósfera, lo que la hacía muy diferente a como es hoy. Los científicos han estudiado cuándo y cómo aumentaron los niveles de oxígeno, ayudando a que la vida se volviera más compleja.

**Qué pasó** – Dos investigadores de la Universidad de Tecnología de Chengdu analizaron rocas antiguas de una forma nueva. En lugar de enfocarse en la química del océano, estudiaron sulfatos que guardan pistas sobre el oxígeno atmosférico. Sus hallazgos muestran que el oxígeno en la atmósfera aumentó en tres etapas principales: hace entre 2.4 y 2.1 mil millones de años, entre 1.3 y 1.0 mil millones de años, y entre 440 y 410 millones de años. Sin embargo, los océanos tardaron mucho más — a veces cientos de millones de años — en llenarse de oxígeno después de la atmósfera.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación cambia cómo entendemos la historia del oxígeno en la Tierra. Muestra que la atmósfera se enriqueció con oxígeno mucho antes que los océanos profundos. Esta demora ayuda a explicar por qué la vida compleja tardó en desarrollarse y por qué algunas señales antiguas de oxígeno fueron engañosas. También revela que existían pequeños oasis ricos en oxígeno en los océanos hace miles de millones de años, cuando la mayoría del planeta tenía poco oxígeno.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos usarán esta nueva cronología para repensar cómo el oxígeno moldeó la evolución de la vida. Buscarán más evidencias químicas detalladas para llenar vacíos y entender mejor el papel del oxígeno en el pasado de la Tierra. Esto podría llevar a nuevos descubrimientos sobre cómo la vida sobrevivió y cambió con los niveles variables de oxígeno.

**Una frase clave** – Nuevas pruebas muestran que la atmósfera de la Tierra ganó oxígeno mucho antes que los océanos profundos, cambiando nuestra comprensión de cómo el oxígeno impulsó la aparición de vida compleja.

articles.title: Press release - MEPs support new measures to protect the EU’s organic agriculture sector
articles.summary: Οn Tuesday, Parliament gave its final green light to update rules governing support for European producers of organic food.Committee on Agriculture and Rural Development Source : © European Union, 2026 - EP
articles.content:
The law, already agreed by Parliament and Council negotiators, will strengthen the protection of both consumers and operators. It was adopted with 486 votes in favour, 39 against and 140 abstentions.

New labelling standards for products from non-EU countries

Under the agreed text, products imported from non-EU countries may use the EU organic production logo in their labelling, presentation, and advertising only if they comply with equivalent standards and where applicable, meet additional production and control requirements of those produced in the EU. These provisions aim to reinforce consumer confidence in organic food and create a level playing field for EU and non-EU producers.

Exemptions for small operators selling directly to consumers

Small businesses selling unpackaged organic products directly to consumers may be exempt from organic certification procedures, provided they sell up to 10,000 kg a year and their annual turnover is below €40,000. These figures have been doubled (from 5,000 kg and €20,000) to enable more small producers to benefit.

Best practices to address cross-contamination

To tackle cross-contamination between organic and non-organic crops, and address divergent member state interpretations, from 31 December 2031 the Commission will publish guidance on best practices for preventing cross-contamination in EU farms.

Quote

Rapporteur Camilla Laureti (S&D, IT) said: “My aim is to give this vital sector a stable, coherent, and predictable regulatory framework. One that simplifies existing requirements while avoiding repeated legislative revisions after its introduction. Regulatory stability is essential to maintaining the high standards that underpin the sector’s quality, competitiveness, and reputation, both within the EU and internationally. The sector must continue to provide robust protection for consumers. Alongside the regulatory framework, to achieve the EU objectives for organic production, we need investment and support too. This is the role of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy and the work that still lies ahead of us. ”

Next steps

The provisional agreement must now be formally endorsed by the Council. Once adopted, the regulation will enter into force one day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

Background

Following a Court of Justice judgment on 4 October 2024 stating that imported products recognised under equivalence arrangements cannot use the EU organic logo, the Commission proposed adjustments to improve clarity for consumers and prevent trade disruptions.

A Eurobarometer survey carried out in 2024 found that the EU organic production logo is the most widely recognised food label among Europeans. The logo helps consumers identify organic products and helps producers market them across the EU.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the EU Parliament's adoption of updated regulations to protect and strengthen the organic agriculture sector, including stricter labeling standards for imports, exemptions to support small producers, and measures to prevent cross-contamination. These changes have broad positive impacts on consumer protection, fair trade, and sustainable agriculture across the EU, with clear and substantive details provided.
articles.personality_title: EU Parliament approves stronger rules to protect organic farming and consumers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The European Union has been working to improve rules for organic farming to protect both farmers and shoppers who choose organic food. Recent court decisions made it necessary to clarify how organic products, especially those imported from outside the EU, are labeled.

**What happened** – On Tuesday, the European Parliament voted to update the rules for organic food. The new law, passed with 486 votes in favor, sets stricter standards for products imported into the EU. Only imports that meet the same strict organic rules as EU products can use the EU organic logo. Small farmers who sell organic products directly to customers can now be exempt from some certification rules if they sell less than 10,000 kg or earn under €40,000 a year—double the previous limits. Also, starting in 2031, the EU will provide guidance to farms on how to avoid mixing organic and non-organic crops.

**Impact** – These changes help shoppers trust that organic products meet high standards, whether they come from inside or outside the EU. Small farmers benefit by having simpler rules, making it easier for them to sell organic food. The rules also help prevent accidental contamination between organic and non-organic crops, keeping organic food pure. Together, these measures support fair trade and protect the reputation of organic farming across Europe.

**What's next step** – The new rules now need approval from the EU Council. Once officially adopted, they will become law shortly after being published. The EU will continue to support organic farming through investments and policies to help farmers meet these standards.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The EU has strengthened rules to protect organic farming, making sure products are genuinely organic and supporting small producers while helping consumers trust what they buy.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Parlement européen adopte des règles renforcées pour protéger l'agriculture biologique et les consommateurs
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L'Union européenne travaille à améliorer les règles pour l'agriculture biologique afin de protéger les agriculteurs et les consommateurs qui choisissent des aliments biologiques. Des décisions récentes de justice ont rendu nécessaire une clarification sur l'étiquetage des produits biologiques, notamment ceux importés.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Mardi, le Parlement européen a voté une mise à jour des règles pour les aliments biologiques. La nouvelle loi, adoptée avec 486 voix pour, établit des normes plus strictes pour les produits importés dans l'UE. Seuls les produits respectant les mêmes règles strictes que les produits européens peuvent utiliser le logo biologique de l'UE. Les petits agriculteurs vendant directement aux clients peuvent désormais être exemptés de certaines procédures de certification s'ils vendent moins de 10 000 kg ou gagnent moins de 40 000 € par an, soit le double des limites précédentes. De plus, à partir de 2031, l'UE publiera des conseils pour aider les exploitations à éviter la contamination croisée entre cultures biologiques et non biologiques.

**Impact** – Ces changements renforcent la confiance des consommateurs dans les produits biologiques, qu'ils viennent de l'UE ou de l'extérieur. Les petits producteurs bénéficient de règles simplifiées, ce qui facilite la vente de produits biologiques. Les règles aident aussi à prévenir la contamination accidentelle, garantissant la pureté des aliments biologiques. Ensemble, ces mesures soutiennent un commerce équitable et protègent la réputation de l'agriculture biologique en Europe.

**Prochaine étape** – Les nouvelles règles doivent maintenant être approuvées par le Conseil de l'UE. Une fois adoptées, elles entreront en vigueur peu après leur publication. L'UE continuera à soutenir l'agriculture biologique par des investissements et des politiques pour aider les agriculteurs.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – L'UE renforce les règles pour protéger l'agriculture biologique, garantir l'authenticité des produits et soutenir les petits producteurs tout en aidant les consommateurs à faire confiance aux aliments qu'ils achètent.

articles.title: A walkable city of tomorrow is growing in suburban Utah
articles.content:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and The Salt Lake Tribune, a nonprofit newsroom in Utah.​​ ​​​​​ ​​ ​​​​​

Sarah Miller biked with her 5-year-old son on a hot afternoon this summer to a vibrant new park in Utah City, a community rising on 700 acres in the heart of Vineyard, one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, and envisioned as its new downtown.

They rode along the Greenline, a wide promenade flanked by pickleball, tennis, and basketball courts that runs through the development, from the FrontRunner train station toward glittering Utah Lake. Miller said she moved with her kids a few ago to live by the lakeshore, and she’s enjoyed watching Utah City go up near her home.

Its first two swanky apartment complexes, called simply 120 and 220 Bend, were finished in February, though only a few balconies had patio furniture. Miller and her son had the park, with its array of slides and wooden play structures to explore, almost to themselves.

“It’s very quiet for now,” Miller said. “I imagine as it grows, more people will come in, and it will feel a bit more alive, but I think it’s beautiful.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Utah City’s developer is building on a rare opportunity to create a transit-oriented, high-density community from scratch in the middle of one of the country’s fastest-growing metro areas — with strong support from former Vineyard city officials, new tools from the local government to help with financing, and investments from taxpayers. It currently has 1,400 units for rent.

The new community has spread across property that was once home to Geneva Steel, an industrial complex built during World War II that went defunct in the 2000s. Former Vineyard officials created tax incentives to clean up the site and agreed to allow the construction of thousands of housing units and high-rise buildings in hopes of luring developers. The Utah Transit Authority built a stop at the site in 2022 for FrontRunner, the commuter train that runs along the Wasatch Front, the state’s urban corridor.

Flagborough LLC, the primary developer of Utah City, says it’s setting an example of how Utah and other Western states can abandon suburban sprawl, with a downtown designed for pedestrians instead of cars and a solution to the smog that plagues the region every summer and winter. They promise that it will be the most ambitious transit-oriented community in the state, with thousands of housing units, limited only by the cost of constructing high-rises.

“The biggest benefit of this project, the greatest opportunity, is that the project’s so big,” said Nate Hutchinson, a partner in both The Flagship Companies, one of the largest housing developers in the state, and Flagborough. They expect to finish building Utah City in 15 to 20 years.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“We’ve been working with a lot of people who’ve done this really well all over the country,” said Pete Evans, a co-managing partner of Utah City and Flagship. “We think we have a pretty good formula on how to make it viable.”

But Utah City is facing heightened scrutiny from a new mayor of Vineyard and new City Council members who say they have a mandate from voters to roll back policies they consider too deferential to developers. They’re skeptical of the vision for Utah City and the leeway and incentives provided to its developer. “Maybe it can work, maybe it can’t,” said Jacob Wood, a Vineyard City Council member who took office in January. “It’s a gamble, but they shouldn’t be gambling with city money.”



David Lauret, another Vineyard City Council member who took office this year, questions whether too many public resources have been committed to Utah City. City Council members also complain about the project’s dense clusters of units for rent, which are partly funded using property tax incentives.



“The problem we have is many of the citizens feel they’re trying to use our money … toward building their business,” Lauret said. “It’s all rental facilities. We’re basically helping to hand them a business they’ll make money with in perpetuity.”

The city paid $4.5 million to Utah City developers in 2026 alone, and council members interviewed for this story said they’re reviewing what those payments covered.

People enjoy a block party at Utah City in Vineyard on Saturday, July 18, 2026. Francisco Kjolseth / The Salt Lake Tribune

Bella’s Market, a grocery store with sparkling floor-to-ceiling glass windows, opened in Utah City late last year across the street from the FrontRunner train station. Next door is the newly opened Fini Pizza, a slice shop recruited from New York City.

Utah City’s water-wise landscaping and green spaces have communal firepits and clusters of chairs under candy-striped sun umbrellas. At the end of the Greenline walkway lies the Utah City playground, topped by a spherical — and climbable — centerpiece that seemingly floats like a hot-air balloon. Taken together, the development has the feel of a vintage boardwalk or century-old World’s Fair promenade, minus the crowds.



These are welcome amenities for Vineyard, which has surged from a sleepy town of 139 in 2010 to a city of about 16,000 today.



Gently curving paseos beckon pedestrians to discover what’s ahead — usually a small plaza with more common spaces. In apartment buildings, board games, books, and vinyl records are neatly arranged in the lobbies.



“The community’s rad,” said Cameron Larsen, a 34-year-old father of four who moved into a three-bedroom apartment with his family in Utah City last February. “The units are pretty bougie.”

Larsen was about to start a new office job, and expected to take the FrontRunner for his commute. His wife, 29-year-old Aunica Larsen, walks to work at Bella’s Market. “This is literally my favorite place I’ve ever lived,” she said. “It’s all very vibey.”

The developers have thrown in all kinds of perks to lure residents, including ski passes to Sundance Mountain Resort and unlimited access to a nearby Peloton fitness center as well as a future swimming pool.

Strolling or cycling through it all, visitors and residents likely won’t think much about dodging cars, let alone traffic. That’s a big win, according to Jeff Speck, a lauded urban designer that Flagship tapped for the project.



“The question isn’t getting Americans to give up their cars. It’s creating an environment in which they just want to use them less,” said Speck, who wrote the 2012 book Walkable City: How Downtown Saves America, One Step at a Time.

New Urbanists like Speck praise neighborhoods that include homes for the wealthy next to homes for the working class and civic buildings like town halls. The cities they favor usually have a European mix of narrow streets, bike paths and sidewalks, and look a lot like the American towns built in the 18th and 19th centuries before cars rose to prominence in Western life.

Utah City has transformed from a sleepy town of hundreds to a city of thousands, as developers reimagine the former site of Geneva Steel, Wednesday, Jan. 21, 2026. Francisco Kjolseth / The Salt Lake Tribune

When it was still just an idea, building Utah City enjoyed widespread support from Vineyard’s elected officials. In 2022, Vineyard applied for a special state designation for the project and succeeded in making it a Housing and Transit Reinvestment Zone. The zones encourage multifamily residential and commercial clusters around transit hubs.



In these zones, as land values climb and revenue rises from property taxes, local governments use the income to pay developers to fund infrastructure like parking garages and utilities, as well as “vertical construction costs” (the additional expense of building above four stories) for up to 25 years. But members of the new City Council doubt high-rise, high-density housing can work surrounded by Utah County’s ever-expanding freeways, frequent gridlock, and seas of subdivisions with single-family homes.

Vineyard’s new mayor, Zack Stratton, called plans to construct more buildings in Utah City “ambitious” but unwelcome. “This is the reality: No one up and down the Wasatch Front wants density.”

In some ways, it’s an old story in a new location.

“Planners go in with the best intentions,” said Sarah Moser, a professor of urban and cultural geography at McGill University in Montreal. “Everyone wants mixed-use, dense, walkable, bikeable cities, but the population is not there.”

People like the idea of riding bikes or taking trains, but when presented with the option, many prefer to stick to their cars. That may especially be the case for Utah residents who are drawn to the state because of activities where a car is necessary — like skiing or visiting national parks.



In 2023, 78 percent of Americans and closer to 79 percent of Utahns drove to work, according to U.S. Census Bureau estimates. In Utah County, just under 66 percent of its more urban population drives alone to work. Only 10 percent of Utah County workers carpool, and less than 2 percent take public transportation.

Moser said she sees a lot of parallels between Utah City and a development in Saudi Arabia called King Abdullah Economic City. Both seek to build vibrant communities centered around public transit that are walkable, dense, and safe.

“They had a hell of a time,” Moser said, “because, well, Saudis don’t like density. They want to be able to drive. It’s prestigious. It’s part of their culture.” Announced in 2005, plans for King Abdullah Economic City called for housing 2 million people. It only managed to attract around 10,000 by 2024, according to a report in Interesting Engineering.

Meanwhile Orem, which borders Vineyard, decided it was done with multifamily, dense rental properties last year and now prioritizes building more single-family homes.

It isn’t just conservative communities in Utah that are balking at transit-focused master planning. California Forever, an eco-friendly, New Urbanist city that would be built from the ground up near San Francisco, remains stymied despite backing by Silicon Valley investors. Residents there keep rejecting it, even after the developers added a train to the plans and spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to persuade them.

Walkways between townhomes and apartments at Utah City in Vineyard, imagined after “paseos,” Spanish for walking paths and promenades, are pictured on Wednesday, Jan. 21, 2026. Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune

In a promotional video for Utah City released earlier this year, the developers boasted that they were creating a place where “people will pay a premium to live.” That’s another concern new Vineyard council members say they have: affordability.

“They’re in the market of selling a luxury lifestyle,” said Wood, the council member.

He figures most students and young professionals in the area can’t afford to live in Utah City. Studio units in the two apartment buildings range from $1,325 to $1,410 a month. Two-bedroom units start around $2,500. That rent does not include parking, extra fees for pets, or most utilities, and it’s based on a 17-month lease.

By contrast, the average rent for a studio in Provo, the county seat and home of Brigham Young University, is $1,199 as of late September, according to Rent.com, while the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment there is $1,521. Utah, like many Western states, faces an affordability crisis. Voters in the state identified the rising cost of living as one of their primary concerns in a 2024 poll by the Utah Foundation, a nonprofit research organization. In July, the average price of a home in Utah was about $585,000 — making it the 10th most expensive market in the country.

Wood, 25, said he would like to buy a house one day, but with his only income coming from his tech business making apps and websites, homeownership feels increasingly out of reach. He said he wants the developers to build commercial spaces for budget-friendly retail stores, too, like a Ross Dress for Less.

“Walkability I don’t care about,” Wood said. “[It] forces a lifestyle the average person isn’t living. Most people drive a car.”

In Vineyard’s application to create the housing and transit zone, the city, Flagship, and other supporters said that increasing the availability of lower-cost housing was a key objective for Utah City. It would include “2,000+” attainable units, which cost 30 percent or less of a household’s income, the application said, and “thousands of housing units” near the FrontRunner stop with “affordable Utah County rents.”



Another City Council member, Jacob Holdaway, is a descendant of the Mormon pioneer family that settled Vineyard and named it after table grapes they grew. He dislikes how past city administrations have guided the city’s growth and has helped lead a community movement that’s wary of developers. He wants to see more homes for sale in Utah City, not rentals.

“When you hear the sales pitch, you’re sold on the thing,” Holdaway said of Utah City’s pitch about its housing. “It was a complete bait and switch. They put this carrot in front of you, and it never happens.”

The developers say they plan to construct “thousands” of housing units, including ones that residents can buy instead of rent; they just want to build the surrounding parks, shops, and eateries first.

“That was always the plan,” said Hutchinson, from Flagship. “To say it’s a bait and switch … is factually not even close to being true.”

Hutchinson said the project is defining what’s affordable based on a standard from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which says low-income households are those that make up to 80 percent of area median income. In Utah County, “low income” means having an annual income of $95,350 or less for a four-person family and $66,750 for a single person.

For this population, Hutchinson said, almost all of the current units are affordable.

“No other group has built more housing in Utah County than we have over the last few years,” he said. “We live in Utah County and care deeply about its future.



Apartment buildings near completion in Utah City alongside courts for basketball, pickleball, tennis on Wednesday, Jan. 21, 2026. Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune

Vineyard’s Redevelopment Agency also provides financial support to Utah City, such as paying for the cleanup of the old Geneva steel mill, which once covered nearly 2,000 acres.



An investigation by the Utah State Auditor last year found that the agency hadn’t properly reported big payments to developers citywide, while a city-commissioned audit found poor oversight and money management. Utah City isn’t specifically named in the state audit, but Vineyard officials said they still can’t say how much taxpayer money the agency has paid developers, including those behind Utah City.



In a controversial move, the City Council recently hired a panel of residents to probe the redevelopment agency’s past contracts and payments, including those tied to Utah City. So far, nothing suspicious has turned up, said Lauret, the council member. “Have we uncovered anything earth shaking? No.”



Vineyard once planned to build a $35 million city hall in Utah City as a civic anchor, but Stratton, the new mayor, led a signature-gathering effort against it. The developers had intended to donate land for the project, but opponents decried the building as too expensive and the prior mayor and council abandoned the idea.

A former council member, Ezra Nair, who also worked as Vineyard’s city manager from February 2022 until November 2023, publicly supported the Utah City development. And he still does.

“Unfortunately, it’s a lot easier to get people angry about something than to get people excited about something,” Nair said. “Building takes time, but tearing down goes really fast.”

As of mid-November, one of the development’s rental buildings is almost full, and the leasing of its 1,400 existing units has been “ahead of pace,” Hutchinson said. He expects more buildings to become available to renters in the next few months.

But a New Urbanism win, the developers caution, takes time, vision, and careful planning. Meanwhile, Utah’s population is booming, and lawmakers are prepared to spend nearly $4 billion to expand the Interstate 15 corridor to keep up with demand. But Utah can’t keep shelling out millions to expand freeways forever, Hutchinson said. The state, for instance, invested more than $1 billion a decade ago on the commuter train, which runs 82 miles from Ogden to Provo.

“It already exists,” Hutchinson said. “The question is, ‘OK, why don’t more people use FrontRunner?’”

The developers believe Utah City offers a solution — with not just a park-and-ride for commuters, but also housing that’s within an easy walk or bike ride away, along with restaurants and stores that make the Vineyard stop a destination in itself. Hutchinson, however, declined to put a number on how many people Utah City could accommodate in the next two decades at full build.

“[The] market will ultimately dictate that,” he said via text message. “It’s unlimited height and unlimited density.”

In 2028, Utah City will be home to a Huntsman Cancer Institute hospital and research facility, which is expected to create around 450 new jobs in research and clinical care. The developers expect to build light industrial and biomedical facilities on the east side of the FrontRunner tracks that would complement a future Utah Valley University campus.

Even skeptics of Utah City call the hospital and university big wins. “That’s exciting for the state,” Stratton said, “exciting for our city.”
